questions.stem: The independent variable in this core practical is:

options.explanation: That is the measured outcome, the dependent variable.
Shape is deliberately changed between trials.
Beam width is a control variable.
Frequency is controlled, not changed.
The perspex material stays the same throughout.
That is an environmental condition, not the measured variable.
The experiment observes how rays redirect.
Blocks are changed one at a time by shape, not counted.

questions.stem: Which is a control variable in this experiment?

options.explanation: That is the independent variable.
That is the dependent variable.
Paper is equipment, not a listed control.

options.text: the width of the light beam
options.explanation: Beam width is held fixed across trials.

questions.stem: After marking where the ray enters and exits the block, the next geometric step is:

options.text: draw dashed normals at right angles to the block outline at the marked points
options.explanation: Normals are needed before any angles can be compared.
The paper carries the whole record.

options.text: switch off the ray box immediately
options.explanation: More rays are still to be traced.
Mass plays no role in the ray geometry.

questions.stem: The blocks are traced onto paper before the ray is fired because:

options.text: tracing makes the block refract more
options.explanation: Drawing cannot change the physics.
Colour is irrelevant.

options.text: the outline preserves the block position so entry and exit points can be joined after removal
options.explanation: Removing the block needs a positional record to reconstruct the geometry.

options.text: the ray box requires an outline to work
options.explanation: The ray box operates independently.

questions.stem: State the independent and dependent variables of this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: Independent: the shape of the block. Dependent: the direction of refraction.

questions.stem: Name the equipment that provides the narrow light beam.
questions.modelAnswer: A ray box provides the narrow beam.

questions.stem: Explain why the same frequency of light is used for every block.
questions.modelAnswer: Frequency is a control variable: changing it would alter the refraction comparison, so keeping it fixed means any differences in ray direction can be attributed to the block shape alone.

questions.stem: A student completes the rectangular block trial and now repeats with the semi-circular block. Describe the repetition steps in order.
questions.modelAnswer: Place the semi-circular block on fresh paper and draw around it, direct the ray box beam at its curved or flat face, mark the entry and exit points plus a point on the exit ray, draw the dashed normals, remove the block, join the points with straight lines, and repeat at another angle of incidence.

questions.stem: A wrongly drawn 90-degree normal line is classified as:

options.explanation: Random errors scatter unpredictably; this one repeats.
The bias repeats on every measurement in the same direction.
It is a measurement issue, not a hazard.
Wrong perpendiculars bias every angle measured from them.

questions.stem: Which fix addresses the systematic error of this experiment?

options.explanation: That reduces random reading scatter, not the systematic bias.
Gloves are a safety measure here, not a geometric fix.
Repetition averages random scatter; it cannot fix a biased construction.

options.text: using a set square to draw the perpendicular lines
options.explanation: The set square makes the normals genuinely ninety degrees.

questions.stem: The protractor resolution of one degree contributes:

options.text: a random error in reading the angles
options.explanation: Instrument resolution scatters individual readings unpredictably.
Resolution limits precision rather than biasing one way.
Protractors are harmless.
Resolution is a measurement limit, not a control issue.

questions.stem: Why should a sharpened pencil mark the middle of the light beam?

options.explanation: The purpose is measurement quality.
Beam width is controlled, not enlarged.

options.text: to reduce random error from inaccurately placed points
options.explanation: Beam-centre marking keeps the traced ray true to the actual path.
This fix targets random placement scatter.

questions.stem: Which safety measure matches the burn risk of the ray box?

options.text: looking into the light to check it works
options.explanation: Looking into the beam is explicitly against the safety rules.
Liquids are kept away from the electrical equipment.

options.text: standing in front of the ray box
options.explanation: You stand behind it, out of the beam.

options.text: running any burn under cold water for at least five minutes
options.explanation: That is the stated response if the hot lamp surface burns skin.

questions.stem: State the three safety considerations of this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The ray box can burn skin, so run burns under cold water for five minutes; never look into the light and stand behind the ray box; keep liquids well clear of any electrical equipment and of the paper.

questions.stem: State how the traced paths are made comparable across angles.
questions.modelAnswer: Each path is labelled clearly, for example (1), (2), (3) or A, B, C, so the refraction angles for different incidence angles can be told apart.

questions.stem: Explain why repeating the procedure at several angles of incidence strengthens the investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: Multiple labelled paths show how the refraction direction responds as the incidence angle changes, turning a single observation into a pattern and letting random marking scatter be seen and averaged out.

questions.stem: A student notices every measured refraction angle is about two degrees too small. Classify the error, propose the most likely cause from this experiment and its fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The consistent one-way offset is a systematic error; the likely cause is the perpendicular lines being drawn slightly off ninety degrees, and the fix is drawing the normals with a set square.
